source: Next morning, Monday, after disposing of the embalmed head to a barber, for a block, I settled my own and comrade’s bill; using, however, my comrade’s money. The grinning landlord, as well as the boarders, seemed amazingly tickled at the sudden friendship which had sprung up between me and Queequeg—especially as Peter Coffin’s cock and bull stories about him had previously so much alarmed me concerning the very person whom I now companied with.

We borrowed a wheelbarrow, and embarking our things, including my own poor carpet-bag, and Queequeg’s canvas sack and hammock, away we went down to “the Moss,” the little Nantucket packet schooner moored at the wharf. As we were going along the people stared; not at Queequeg so much—for they were used to seeing cannibals like him in their streets,—but at seeing him and me upon such confidential terms. But we heeded them not, going along wheeling the barrow by turns, and Queequeg now and then stopping to adjust the sheath on his harpoon barbs. I asked him why he carried such a troublesome thing with him ashore, and whether all whaling ships did not find their own harpoons. To this, in substance, he replied, that though what I hinted was true enough, yet he had a particular affection for his own harpoon, because it was of assured stuff, well tried in many a mortal combat, and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales. In short, like many inland reapers and mowers, who go into the farmers’ meadows armed with their own scythes—though in no wise obliged to furnish them—even so, Queequeg, for his own private reasons, preferred his own harpoon.

Shifting the barrow from my hand to his, he told me a funny story about the first wheelbarrow he had ever seen. It was in Sag Harbor. The owners of his ship, it seems, had lent him one, in which to carry his heavy chest to his boarding house. Not to seem ignorant about the thing—though in truth he was entirely so, concerning the precise way in which to manage the barrow—Queequeg puts his chest upon it; lashes it fast; and then shoulders the barrow and marches up the wharf. “Why,” said I, “Queequeg, you might have known better than that, one would think. Didn’t the people laugh?”

Upon this, he told me another story. The people of his island of Rokovoko, it seems, at their wedding feasts express the fragrant water of young cocoanuts into a large stained calabash like a punchbowl; and this punchbowl always forms the great central ornament on the braided mat where the feast is held. Now a certain grand merchant ship once touched at Rokovoko, and its commander—from all accounts, a very stately punctilious gentleman, at least for a sea captain—this commander was invited to the wedding feast of Queequeg’s sister, a pretty young princess just turned of ten. Well; when all the wedding guests were assembled at the bride’s bamboo cottage, this Captain marches in, and being assigned the post of honor, placed himself over against the punchbowl, and between the High Priest and his majesty the King, Queequeg’s father. Grace being said,—for those people have their grace as well as we—though Queequeg told me that unlike us, who at such times look downwards to our platters, they, on the contrary, copying the ducks, glance upwards to the great Giver of all feasts—Grace, I say, being said, the High Priest opens the banquet by the immemorial ceremony of the island; that is, dipping his consecrated and consecrating fingers into the bowl before the blessed beverage circulates. Seeing himself placed next the Priest, and noting the ceremony, and thinking himself—being Captain of a ship—as having plain precedence over a mere island King, especially in the King’s own house—the Captain coolly proceeds to wash his hands in the punchbowl;—taking it I suppose for a huge finger-glass. “Now,” said Queequeg, “what you tink now?—Didn’t our people laugh?”

At last, passage paid, and luggage safe, we stood on board the schooner. Hoisting sail, it glided down the Acushnet river. On one side, New Bedford rose in terraces of streets, their ice-covered trees all glittering in the clear, cold air. Huge hills and mountains of casks on casks were piled upon her wharves, and side by side the world-wandering whale ships lay silent and safely moored at last; while from others came a sound of carpenters and coopers, with blended noises of fires and forges to melt the pitch, all betokening that new cruises were on the start; that one most perilous and long voyage ended, only begins a second; and a second ended, only begins a third, and so on, for ever and for aye. Such is the endlessness, yea, the intolerableness of all earthly effort.

Gaining the more open water, the bracing breeze waxed fresh; the little Moss tossed the quick foam from her bows, as a young colt his snortings. How I snuffed that Tartar air!—how I spurned that turnpike earth!—that common highway all over dented with the marks of slavish heels and hoofs; and turned me to admire the magnanimity of the sea which will permit no records.

At the same foam-fountain, Queequeg seemed to drink and reel with me. His dusky nostrils swelled apart; he showed his filed and pointed teeth. On, on we flew; and our offing gained, the Moss did homage to the blast; ducked and dived her bows as a slave before the Sultan. Sideways leaning, we sideways darted; every ropeyarn tingling like a wire; the two tall masts buckling like Indian canes in land tornadoes. So full of this reeling scene were we, as we stood by the plunging bowsprit, that for some time we did not notice the jeering glances of the passengers, a lubber-like assembly, who marvelled that two fellow beings should be so companionable; as though a white man were anything more dignified than a whitewashed negro. But there were some boobies and bumpkins there, who, by their intense greenness, must have come from the heart and centre of all verdure. Queequeg caught one of these young saplings mimicking him behind his back. I thought the bumpkin’s hour of doom was come. Dropping his harpoon, the brawny savage caught him in his arms, and by an almost miraculous dexterity and strength, sent him high up bodily into the air; then slightly tapping his stern in mid-somerset, the fellow landed with bursting lungs upon his feet, while Queequeg, turning his back upon him, lighted his tomahawk pipe and passed it to me for a puff.
“Capting! Capting!” yelled the bumpkin, running towards that officer; “Capting, Capting, here’s the devil.”
“Hallo, you sir,” cried the Captain, a gaunt rib of the sea, stalking up to Queequeg, “what in thunder do you mean by that? Don’t you know you might have killed that chap?”
“What him say?” said Queequeg, as he mildly turned to me.
“He say,” said I, “that you came near kill-e that man there,” pointing to the still shivering greenhorn.
“Kill-e,” cried Queequeg, twisting his tattooed face into an unearthly expression of disdain, “ah! him bevy small-e fish-e; Queequeg no kill-e so small-e fish-e; Queequeg kill-e big whale!”
“Look you,” roared the Captain, “I’ll kill-e you, you cannibal, if you try any more of your tricks aboard here; so mind your eye.”

But it so happened just then, that it was high time for the Captain to mind his own eye. The prodigious strain upon the main-sail had parted the weather-sheet, and the tremendous boom was now flying from side to side, completely sweeping the entire after part of the deck. The poor fellow whom Queequeg had handled so roughly, was swept overboard; all hands were in a panic; and to attempt snatching at the boom to stay it, seemed madness. It flew from right to left, and back again, almost in one ticking of a watch, and every instant seemed on the point of snapping into splinters. Nothing was done, and nothing seemed capable of being done; those on deck rushed towards the bows, and stood eyeing the boom as if it were the lower jaw of an exasperated whale. In the midst of this consternation, Queequeg dropped deftly to his knees, and crawling under the path of the boom, whipped hold of a rope, secured one end to the bulwarks, and then flinging the other like a lasso, caught it round the boom as it swept over his head, and at the next jerk, the spar was that way trapped, and all was safe. The schooner was run into the wind, and while the hands were clearing away the stern boat, Queequeg, stripped to the waist, darted from the side with a long living arc of a leap. For three minutes or more he was seen swimming like a dog, throwing his long arms straight out before him, and by turns revealing his brawny shoulders through the freezing foam. I looked at the grand and glorious fellow, but saw no one to be saved. The greenhorn had gone down. Shooting himself perpendicularly from the water, Queequeg, now took an instant’s glance around him, and seeming to see just how matters were, dived down and disappeared. A few minutes more, and he rose again, one arm still striking out, and with the other dragging a lifeless form. The boat soon picked them up. The poor bumpkin was restored. All hands voted Queequeg a noble trump; the captain begged his pardon. From that hour I clove to Queequeg like a barnacle; yea, till poor Queequeg took his last long dive.

Was there ever such unconsciousness? He did not seem to think that he at all deserved a medal from the Humane and Magnanimous Societies. He only asked for water—fresh water—something to wipe the brine off; that done, he put on dry clothes, lighted his pipe, and leaning against the bulwarks, and mildly eyeing those around him, seemed to be saying to himself—“It’s a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians. We cannibals must help these Christians.”

modern_da.title: Kapitel 13 — Trillebør
paragraphs: Næste morgen, mandag, efter at jeg havde solgt det balsamerede hoved til en barber til brug som parykblok, gjorde jeg min egen og min kammerats regning op — dog med min kammerats penge. Den grinende vært og de andre gæster syntes at more sig vildt over det pludselige venskab, der var opstået mellem mig og Queequeg — især fordi Peter Coffins skrøverhistorier om ham tidligere havde gjort mig så bange for netop den person, jeg nu var sammen med.

Vi lånte en trillebør, og da vi havde læsset vores ting på den, heriblandt min egen stakkels tæppetaske og Queequegs lærredssæk og hængekøje, drog vi af sted ned til »Moss«, den lille skonnert fra Nantucket, der sejlede med post og passagerer og lå fortøjet ved kajen. Mens vi gik, stirrede folk — ikke så meget på Queequeg, for de var vant til at se kannibaler som ham på deres gader, men på at se ham og mig på så fortrolig fod. Men vi var ligeglade med dem og gik og trillede børen på skift, mens Queequeg af og til stoppede for at rette på skeden om sine harpunhager. Jeg spurgte ham, hvorfor han bar rundt på sådan en besværlig ting i land, og om ikke alle hvalfangerskibe selv leverede harpuner. Hertil svarede han i grunden, at selv om det, jeg sagde, var sandt nok, havde han en særlig kærlighed til sin egen harpun, for den var lavet af pålideligt stof, prøvet i mangen en dødelig kamp og dybt fortrolig med hvalers hjerter. Kort sagt: ligesom mange landlige høstfolk og slåmænd går ind på bøndernes enge bevæbnet med deres egne leer — selv om de slet ikke er forpligtet til at have dem med — ganske sådan foretrak Queequeg af sine egne private grunde sin egen harpun.

Mens han flyttede børen fra min hånd til sin, fortalte han mig en sjov historie om den første trillebør, han nogensinde havde set. Det var i Sag Harbor. Skibets redere havde, ser det ud til, lånt ham en til at bære hans tunge kiste hen til hans logi. For ikke at se uvidende ud i den sag — selv om han i sandhed var fuldstændig uvidende om, hvordan man håndterer en bør — lægger Queequeg sin kiste op på den, surrer den fast, tager så børen på skulderen og marcherer op ad kajen. »Men Queequeg,« sagde jeg, »det kunne du godt have vidst bedre, skulle man mene. Lo folk ikke?«

Så fortalte han mig en anden historie. Folkene på hans ø, Rokovoko, presser åbenbart saften af unge kokosnødder ud i en stor, plettet kalabas, der ligner en punschebowle, når de holder bryllupsfest. Den bowle er altid det store midtpunkt på den flettede måtte, hvor festen holdes. Nu skete det, at et stort handelsskib engang anløb Rokovoko, og dets chef — efter alt at dømme en meget statelig og nøjeregnende herre, i det mindste til en skibskaptajn at være — blev inviteret med til bryllupsfesten for Queequegs søster, en køn ung prinsesse der lige var fyldt ti. Da alle bryllupsgæsterne var samlet i brudens bambushytte, marcherer kaptajnen ind. Han får hædersplads og sætter sig lige over for bowlen, mellem ypperstepræsten og hans majestæt kongen, Queequegs far. Velsignelsen bliver sagt — for de mennesker har deres bordbøn ligesom vi, selv om Queequeg fortalte mig, at de ikke ser ned i tallerkenen, som vi gør, men tværtimod ser opad mod den store giver af alle fester, ligesom ænderne — da bordbønnen altså er sagt, åbner ypperstepræsten festmåltidet med øens ældgamle ceremoni; det vil sige, at han dypper sine indviede og indviende fingre i bowlen, før den velsignede drik går rundt. Kaptajnen ser, at han sidder ved siden af præsten, og lægger mærke til ceremonien. Han tænker, at han som kaptajn på et skib da må have forrang for en blot og bar ø-konge, og det endda i kongens eget hus, og så går han helt køligt i gang med at vaske hænder i bowlen, fordi han vist tror, at det er en kæmpestor fingerskål. »Nå,« sagde Queequeg, »hvad du tænke nu? Vores folk ikke grine?«

Til sidst, da billetten var betalt og bagagen i sikkerhed, stod vi om bord på skonnerten. Hun hejste sejl og gled ned ad Acushnet-floden. På den ene side steg New Bedford op i terrasser af gader, og de isbelagte træer glimtede i den klare, kolde luft. På kajerne lå enorme bjerge og høje af tønder på tønder, og side om side lå hvalskibene, der sejler jorden rundt, stille og endelig sikkert fortøjet. Fra andre skibe lød larmen fra tømrere og bødkere, blandet med lyden af ildsteder og smedjer, hvor man smeltede beg — alt sammen tegn på, at nye rejser var ved at begynde; at enden på én lang og dybt farlig rejse kun er begyndelsen på en anden, og enden på den anden kun begyndelsen på en tredje, og så fremdeles, evigt og altid. Sådan er alt jordisk arbejdes endeløshed — ja, dets uudholdelighed.

Da vi kom ud på mere åbent vand, blev den friske brise stærkere, og lille Moss kastede det hurtige skum op fra bovene, som et ungt føl kaster sine fnys. Hvor jeg snusede til den tartariske luft! Hvor jeg foragtede den banede jord — den almindelige landevej, der er præget overalt af trællebundne hæle og hove — og vendte mig for at beundre havets storsind, som ikke vil tillade nogen spor.

Queequeg syntes at drikke og svimle sammen med mig ved den samme skumkilde. Hans mørke næsebor svulmede ud til siderne, og han viste sine filede og spidse tænder. Frem, frem fløj vi, og da vi var nået ud på åbent vand, hyldede Moss stormbygen og dykkede og dukkede med bovene som en slave for sultanen. Vi lå på skrå og for af sted på skrå. Hvert eneste rebgarn dirrede som en ståltråd, og de to høje master bøjede sig som indiske rør i tornadoer over land. Vi var så optaget af dette svimlende syn, mens vi stod ved det stampende bovspryd, at vi i nogen tid ikke lagde mærke til passagerernes hånlige blikke. Det var en klodset flok landkrabber, som undrede sig over, at to medmennesker kunne være så gode venner — som om en hvid mand var noget mere værdigt end en hvidkalket sort mand. Men der var nogle tåber og bondeknolde, som ved deres vældige grønhed må være kommet fra selve hjertet og midten af alt grønt, der gror. Queequeg opdagede en af disse unge grene, der gjorde nar af ham bag hans ryg. Jeg troede, at bondeknoldens sidste time var kommet. Den kraftige vilde lod sin harpun falde, tog fat i ham med armene og sendte ham med en næsten mirakuløs behændighed og styrke højt op i luften. Så gav han ham et let klap bagi midt i saltoen, og knægten landede på fødderne med brændende lunger, mens Queequeg vendte ryggen til ham, tændte sin tomahawk-pibe og rakte den til mig for at jeg kunne tage et drag.
»Kaptæn! Kaptæn!« råbte bondeknolden og løb hen imod den mand. »Kaptæn, Kaptæn, her er fanden selv.«
»Hallo, du der, hr.,« råbte kaptajnen, et radmagert ribben af havet, mens han skred hen til Queequeg, »hvad i himlens navn mener du med det? Ved du ikke, at du kunne have slået ham ihjel?«
»Hvad han sige?« sagde Queequeg og vendte sig mildt mod mig.
»Han sige,« sagde jeg, »du næsten dræb-e den mand der,« og pegede på den nybegynder, der stadig rystede.
»Dræb-e,« råbte Queequeg og fordrejede sit tatoverede ansigt til et overjordisk udtryk af foragt, »ah! han meget lille fisk-e; Queequeg ikke dræb-e så lille fisk-e; Queequeg dræb-e stor hval!«
»Hør her,« brølede kaptajnen, »jeg dræb-e dig, din kannibal, hvis du prøver flere af dine kunster her om bord, så pas på.«

Men netop da var det, som det skete, på høje tid, at kaptajnen så sig for. Det enorme træk i storsejlet havde sprængt skødet på luvsiden, og den store bom svang nu vildt fra side til side og fejede hen over hele den bageste del af dækket. Den stakkel, som Queequeg havde behandlet så hårdhændet, blev slået over bord. Hele besætningen gik i panik, og at prøve at gribe fat i bommen for at standse den lignede vanvid. Den fløj fra højre mod venstre og tilbage igen på næsten ikke mere end et enkelt tik af et ur, og hvert øjeblik så den ud til at ville splintres. Ingen gjorde noget, og intet syntes muligt at gøre. Folkene på dækket løb frem mod bovene og stod og stirrede på bommen, som om det var underkæben på en rasende hval. Midt i alarmen faldt Queequeg behændigt på knæ, krøb ind under bommens bane, greb et tov og gjorde den ene ende fast til skansekledningen. Så slyngede han den anden ende som et lasso og fik den fanget om bommen, da den fejede hen over hans hoved. Ved næste ryk var rundholtet fanget, og alt var i sikkerhed. Skonnerten blev drejet op i vinden, og mens besætningen gjorde den agterste båd klar, skød Queequeg, nøgen til livet, af sted fra rælingen i et langt, levende spring i en bue. I tre minutter eller mere kunne man se ham svømme som en hund, med de lange arme kastet lige frem foran sig, og de kraftige skuldre viste sig nu og da gennem det iskolde skum. Jeg så på denne store og herlige mand, men så ingen at redde. Nybegynderen var gået under. Queequeg skød lige op af vandet, kastede et blik rundt omkring sig et øjeblik og dykkede, som om han forstod præcis, hvordan sagen stod, ned og forsvandt. Nogle få minutter senere kom han op igen, med den ene arm stadig svømmende og den anden slæbende på en livløs krop. Båden tog snart begge to op. Den stakkels bondeknold blev bragt til live igen. Hele besætningen erklærede Queequeg for en ædel knægt, og kaptajnen bad ham om tilgivelse. Fra den time hang jeg ved Queequeg som en rur — ja, indtil stakkels Queequeg tog sit sidste lange dyk.

Har der nogensinde været sådan en uselvbevidsthed? Han syntes slet ikke at mene, at han på nogen måde fortjente en medalje fra Selskaberne for Menneskelighed og Storsind. Han bad kun om vand — ferskvand — noget at tørre saltvandet af med. Da det var gjort, tog han tørt tøj på, tændte sin pibe, lænede sig op ad skansekledningen og så mildt på dem rundt om sig, og han så ud til at sige til sig selv: »Det er en gensidig verden med fælles aktier, på alle længdegrader. Vi kannibaler må hjælpe disse kristne.«
